messages.content: I want to develop simultaneous speech translation that preserves late-resolved negation and semantic roles while committing output that cannot be revised, under bounded latency. How should I understand the central difficulty?

The translator has to speak before it has heard the entire source. Some later speech may determine whether an earlier idea is negated, or clarify who did what to whom. If the translation has already committed wording that expresses the wrong meaning, it cannot take that wording back. At the same time, waiting indefinitely for clarification would conflict with bounded latency. The goal is to preserve those meanings despite that tension.
So “late-resolved” does not mean the translator can simply wait until every ambiguity disappears?

Right. It means the information needed to interpret negation or semantic roles may arrive late relative to the point at which output is expected. The task is to handle that situation while still producing irreversible output within a latency bound. The goal does not specify a particular way to decide when to commit.
What counts as preserving negation here?

The committed translation should retain whether the source meaning is affirmative or negative, including when that distinction becomes clear only later. An error would be output that leaves the listener with the wrong polarity. This is about preserving the source meaning, not merely reproducing the position of a negation word.
And semantic roles are about the relationships among the participants in what was said?

Yes. In this goal, preserving semantic roles means keeping straight who is doing something, who or what is affected, and similar relationships conveyed by the speech. Those relationships can be misrepresented if an irreversible translation commits to an interpretation before the relevant source information is available.
Does the goal require eliminating every negation or role error?

No. Its stated comparative requirement is at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline. That is a target for improvement over that baseline, not a claim of zero errors or a claim that the target has already been achieved.
What work is “matched-latency” doing in that comparison?

It keeps the error comparison tied to a streaming baseline operating at matched latency. The intended improvement is not simply the result of allowing the proposed translation to wait longer than its comparator. Separately, the goal requires average lagging below two seconds.
Is “at least 20% fewer” a relative comparison, rather than an instruction to subtract 20 percentage points?

Yes: “20% fewer ... errors than” expresses a relative reduction against the matched-latency streaming baseline. It does not state a 20-percentage-point reduction. Nor does the wording provide a measured baseline error count or report an achieved reduction.
Should I read that as a separate 20% threshold for negation errors and another for role errors?

The stated requirement is “at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline.” It identifies both kinds of error as important, but does not specify here whether the threshold is calculated separately for each kind or over a combined accounting. I would keep that distinction open rather than add a measurement rule that is not stated.
How does the two-second condition fit with bounded latency?

The goal calls for irreversible output under bounded latency and gives a specific performance requirement: average lagging must stay below two seconds. “Average” matters—it is not, by itself, a statement that every individual word or segment has a lag below two seconds. And “below” means strictly less than two seconds, not equal to two seconds.
Could the system satisfy the lagging condition but still fail the goal?

Yes. Average lagging below two seconds is only one requirement. The system must also achieve at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than the matched-latency streaming baseline, without reducing overall COMET versus that same baseline. Meeting the lagging threshold alone would not establish the other conditions.
Why mention overall COMET as well as those specific errors?

The error target focuses on negation and semantic roles, while overall COMET is a broader translation-quality comparison. The requirement prevents an improvement on the specified errors from counting as sufficient if overall COMET is reduced relative to the same matched-latency streaming baseline. It does not say that COMET must increase; no reduction is the stated condition.
Does “overall” imply that every individual translation must have an equal or higher COMET score?

No. The condition is framed in terms of overall COMET versus the baseline, not a guarantee about every individual translation. It also does not supply any COMET scores or specify how individual cases would be distributed.
Let me check the full reading: the system cannot retract output, it must manage meanings that may become clear late, and it cannot buy accuracy by ignoring the latency constraints.

That captures the central tension. More precisely, the development goal is simultaneous speech translation that preserves late-resolved negation and semantic roles while committing irreversible output under bounded latency. Success is constrained by all three stated comparisons: at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline, average lagging below two seconds, and no reduction in overall COMET versus that same baseline.
Is any particular implementation or successful result implied by stating those targets?

No. These are a development goal and requirements, not a report of a completed experiment or a choice of implementation. They specify what the translation should preserve and the conditions under which its performance would need to be assessed, without saying that a system has already met them.
Could we make the simultaneous-translation idea more concrete without assuming that it has already worked?

One proposal is to use ASR-lattice role and negation posteriors to commit safe target prefixes while deferring risky phrases under a 1.8-second hold cap. It describes what information would guide commitments and how long risky material could be held, but it does not report an implementation or a result.
What does the ASR lattice contribute that a single transcription would not?

Conceptually, a lattice retains alternative recognition possibilities rather than treating one transcription as the whole picture. The proposed role and negation posteriors draw on that uncertainty when judging whether a target phrase is safe to commit. The proposal does not specify how those posteriors are computed or how accurate they would be.
Are the posteriors about the words themselves, or about the meaning I would put into the translation?

The proposal specifically calls for role and negation posteriors. Their relevance is semantic: how confident the translator can be about relationships such as who did what, and about whether the meaning is negated. The ASR lattice is the proposed source of information for those judgments; the node does not define a particular probability model.
Why make the commitment unit a target prefix?

Because the output is committed as it is produced. A prefix is the beginning of the target translation that can be delivered now, with later output appended rather than earlier output revised. Calling a prefix safe means it is judged suitable for that irreversible commitment despite the source speech still unfolding; it is not a guarantee that every such judgment will be correct.
Does deferring a risky phrase mean stopping the whole translation until it becomes certain?

Not necessarily. The proposal distinguishes committing safe target prefixes from deferring risky phrases. Its point is that uncertainty about a particular negation or role need not automatically prevent every possible commitment. Whether a useful safe prefix exists in a given moment is another question; the proposal does not promise that one always will.
Can you illustrate the distinction without assuming a particular language pair or translation procedure?

Imagine that a stretch of speech has begun to convey an action, but later speech could determine whether that action is negated. Committing target wording that asserts the action may be risky before that distinction is resolved. If there is earlier target wording whose meaning does not depend on that unresolved distinction, it could be a candidate safe prefix. That is only a conceptual illustration, not a specified rule for finding one.
Would a role ambiguity create the same kind of problem?

Yes. If later speech could clarify which participant performed an action and which was affected, an early target phrase that fixes those roles could be hard to correct after commitment. The proposed role posteriors are meant to inform that decision alongside the negation posteriors.
So a phrase is risky if the lattice leaves open interpretations that would require different target wording?

That is a reasonable way to describe the concern. In particular, alternatives that differ in negation or semantic roles can make irreversible wording risky. The proposal does not, however, specify a formal test for risk, a probability threshold, or how differences among possible target wordings would be evaluated.
Does “safe” require certainty across every ASR alternative?

No such requirement is stated. “Safe target prefixes” names the intended kind of commitment, while the role and negation posteriors suggest decisions informed by degrees of uncertainty. The proposal leaves open exactly how much confidence is sufficient, and it does not establish that the posteriors are perfectly reliable.
What precisely is limited by the 1.8-second figure?

It is a 1.8-second hold cap on deferring risky phrases. The phrasing does not define the exact point from which a hold is timed or a detailed action to take when the cap is reached. What it does rule out is treating deferral as open-ended.
If the uncertainty remains at the cap, can we say the system must output its most likely guess?

We cannot infer that particular behavior from the proposal. The hold cap limits how long a risky phrase is deferred, but no tie-breaking or fallback policy is given for uncertainty that persists. Saying it must make a specific kind of guess would add an implementation decision.
Is the 1.8-second cap just another way to say average lagging is below two seconds?

No. A cap on holding risky phrases and average lagging are different conditions. The proposed 1.8-second hold cap does not by itself establish that the system's average lagging is below two seconds; that remains a separate requirement of the translation goal.
Would these posteriors automatically deliver the required reduction in negation and role errors?

No. They are proposed inputs to commitment decisions, not evidence of a measured improvement. The goal is at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline, while keeping average lagging below two seconds without reducing overall COMET versus that same baseline. The proposal alone establishes none of those outcomes.
Could postponing risky phrases improve the targeted errors but cause a different problem?

It could create a tension with timely output: holding material avoids an immediate irreversible commitment, but time spent waiting matters in simultaneous translation. It is also not enough to consider only negation and role errors, because the goal retains the overall COMET condition. Those are constraints to assess, not effects that this proposal has been shown to produce.
Does the proposal say that negation should be handled before roles, or that one posterior takes priority?

No. It names both role and negation posteriors as information for committing safe prefixes and deferring risky phrases. It does not specify a priority ordering between them or a rule for resolving cases where their implications differ.
I think I understand the balance: make whatever irreversible prefix can be judged safe, hold back wording that might commit to the wrong polarity or roles, and keep that hold bounded.

Yes—that expresses the proposal's intended balance. The distinctive pieces are the ASR-lattice role and negation posteriors, safe target-prefix commitments, deferral of risky phrases, and the 1.8-second hold cap. How safety is judged in detail, what happens if uncertainty persists at the cap, and whether the goal's measured requirements are met are not specified by this proposal.
The open question seems to be whether ASR-lattice posteriors can actually identify target prefixes that remain correct when negation or semantic roles resolve late. Is that the right question?

Yes. It asks whether those posteriors can support a reliable commitment decision, not merely whether they indicate a likely interpretation of the speech heard so far. A target prefix is useful here only if it remains correct after the later information clarifies negation or semantic roles. The question does not assume that ASR-lattice posteriors can identify such prefixes.
Why is identifying the likely interpretation not enough?

Because an irreversible prefix has to withstand what comes next. An interpretation may be likely now yet still turn out to have the wrong polarity or assign the wrong roles. If the committed target wording depends on that interpretation, its likelihood alone does not make the wording safe.
Then is the question really about the target wording, rather than just the source interpretation?

It involves both. The ASR-lattice posteriors concern uncertainty about negation and roles in the source, but the decision is about a target prefix. The key issue is whether the unresolved source possibilities would change the correctness of that particular target wording. Uncertainty in the source does not automatically make every possible prefix wrong, and a plausible source reading does not automatically make a particular prefix safe.
What would it mean for a prefix to “remain correct” after a late resolution?

It would mean that the target words already committed still convey an appropriate meaning when the later speech establishes the negation or semantic roles. Later target words may add information, but they cannot undo a polarity or role assignment that the prefix has already expressed incorrectly.
Could the prefix remain correct if it simply has not expressed the disputed relationship yet?

Conceptually, yes. A prefix that does not commit to the unresolved negation or role might remain compatible with its later resolution. But compatibility has to be judged for the actual target wording: avoiding an explicit negation word, for example, does not necessarily mean the prefix has avoided asserting an affirmative meaning.
So the test is not just whether I can append a correction afterward?

Right. The output is irreversible. If an earlier prefix already tells the listener the wrong thing, appending words later does not make that earlier commitment correct. The question is whether the prefix itself can survive the late resolution without needing revision.
Suppose the posteriors strongly favor one role assignment. Would that identify a safe prefix?

Not necessarily. A strong posterior favors an interpretation; it does not by itself establish that wording committed on that basis will remain correct if the interpretation changes. Conversely, a prefix might be safe because it does not depend on the unresolved role assignment, even if that assignment is uncertain. Whether the posteriors distinguish those situations is part of the open question.
Does that mean safety is always an all-or-nothing property?

For a particular committed prefix and a particular eventual meaning, the question is whether that prefix remains correct. Before the later speech arrives, though, there is uncertainty about which meaning will be established. The node asks whether ASR-lattice posteriors can help identify prefixes that will withstand that uncertainty; it does not specify a certainty threshold or a formal definition of safety.
I can imagine a prefix that is neutral about negation but already fixes who did what. Would it count?

It could still be risky. Remaining correct when negation or semantic roles resolve late requires attention to both. Neutrality about polarity does not protect a prefix that prematurely assigns roles, just as avoiding a role assignment does not protect wording that prematurely asserts an affirmative or negative meaning.
Could different lattice alternatives lead to the same safe target prefix?

That is a possibility the question invites us to consider. Alternatives may differ in details that have not yet been expressed in the target prefix. What matters is whether the committed words remain correct under the late resolution, not whether every source alternative is identical. The node does not say how to determine that correspondence.
And if the alternatives would require incompatible beginnings in the target language?

Then identifying a prefix that remains correct could be difficult, or there might be no useful prefix to commit at that point. That is a conceptual possibility, not a reported finding. The question leaves open when such prefixes exist and whether the posteriors can identify them.
Is an ASR lattice enough on its own to answer a question about a target prefix?

The question does not establish that it is. ASR-lattice posteriors can represent uncertainty relevant to negation and roles, but correctness is a property of the target wording in light of the eventual source meaning. The gap between information about source possibilities and a judgment about an irreversible target prefix is precisely why this is an open question.
Should I read “can” as asking whether this is possible in principle, or whether it works reliably in the translation setting?

The wording asks whether ASR-lattice posteriors can identify prefixes with that property. It does not set out a separate theoretical claim or report a measured level of reliability. In the context of simultaneous translation, the practical concern is whether they can guide commitments that remain correct when the relevant meaning arrives late; how reliably they do so remains unanswered here.
Could a prefix look harmless at the time of commitment but prove wrong only because the later speech changes how an earlier phrase should be understood?

Yes, that is the difficulty captured by “resolve late.” Later information can settle the polarity or role relationships of material already heard. A prefix that seemed compatible with an early interpretation might then prove to have committed to the wrong meaning. The question is whether the posteriors give enough warning before that commitment.
Does the question ask whether posteriors predict the exact future words?

No. It is narrower and more semantic: can they identify target prefixes that remain correct despite a later resolution of negation or roles? Predicting the exact future speech is not stated as the task. The relevant distinction is whether later information can invalidate wording already committed.
Would an answer of “sometimes” settle it?

Not without more qualification. The question concerns whether posteriors can identify prefixes that remain correct in the late-resolution cases at issue. A vague “sometimes” would not explain which commitments they can distinguish from risky ones or how dependable that distinction is. The node provides no evidence from which to settle those points.
How does this connect to deferring risky phrases?

Identifying a safe prefix and recognizing a risky phrase are complementary parts of the proposed commitment decision. If the posteriors cannot distinguish wording that will survive late resolution from wording that will not, they cannot reliably guide that distinction. The open question concerns that identification, not a demonstrated outcome of deferral.
And the 1.8-second hold cap does not answer whether the prefix itself is correct?

Correct. A hold cap limits deferral; it does not establish that the posteriors correctly identify safe target prefixes. A phrase could be held for a bounded time while the underlying judgment about what can be committed remains uncertain. These are related concerns, but the question here is specifically about identifying prefixes that stay correct after late negation or role resolution.
Then the precise question is whether uncertainty represented in an ASR lattice can be turned into a trustworthy judgment about what target words are safe to make irreversible.

Yes, with the emphasis on late-resolved negation and semantic roles. The judgment has to concern the target prefix that would actually be committed, not just confidence in one provisional reading of the source. Whether ASR-lattice posteriors can make that distinction is the question, rather than an established result.
Can we state a more precise hypothesis for whether the lattice gate identifies prefixes that stay correct after late resolution?

The hypothesis is: on late-resolution MuST-C En–De, at least 95% of prefixes passing a 0.9 role-negation lattice gate need no oracle correction. It proposes a measurable answer to the question about safe commitments; it is not a reported result.
What exactly is the 95% a percentage of?

It is a percentage of the target prefixes that pass the 0.9 role-negation lattice gate in that setting. The hypothesis says that at least 95% of those passing prefixes need no oracle correction. It does not say that 95% of all possible prefixes pass the gate.
So it is conditional on passing, not a statement about the whole translation output?

Exactly. The stated group is prefixes passing the gate. A high no-correction rate within that group would not, by itself, say how many prefixes were held back, how much output was committed, or how the complete translations performed.
Does the 0.9 mean that exactly 90% of gated prefixes should be correct?

No. The 0.9 belongs to the role-negation lattice gate, while the predicted outcome is at least 95% needing no oracle correction among prefixes that pass it. The hypothesis does not define the gate's internal calculation, so it would be unwarranted to equate its 0.9 setting with an observed 90% correctness rate.
Is the gate specifically about both role and negation uncertainty?

Yes, it is named a role-negation lattice gate. That connects the hypothesis to the concern that semantic roles or negation may resolve late. The wording does not specify whether the gate combines two posteriors, applies separate conditions, or uses some other detailed calculation.
Why say the prefixes need no oracle correction rather than simply calling them correct?

“Need no oracle correction” is the outcome the hypothesis actually states. It focuses on whether a prefix that passed the gate would have to be changed under an oracle judgment. That is closely related to making an irreversible commitment, but the hypothesis does not supply a detailed definition of the oracle or claim that every aspect of a complete translation is correct.
Is the oracle correction meant to address what happens after the late negation or role information becomes clear?

That is the relevant reading in context: the concern is whether a committed prefix survives late resolution without needing correction. The hypothesis does not describe an oracle procedure or specify every circumstance that would trigger a correction, so those details should remain open.
If a prefix passes the gate and later needs correction, would that contradict the hypothesis?

A single such prefix would not necessarily contradict it. “At least 95%” allows some passing prefixes to need correction. The hypothesis would fail its stated threshold if fewer than 95% of the passing prefixes needed no oracle correction in the specified setting.
And exactly 95% would satisfy it?
Yes. The symbol ≥ includes equality: 95% or more would meet the stated threshold. Anything below 95% would not, assuming the same set of passing prefixes and the same correction judgment.
Does this predict that the gate will pass most prefixes?

No. The hypothesis says nothing about the proportion of prefixes that pass. It could not be used alone to infer how often the translator can commit a prefix. Gate coverage and the no-correction rate among passing prefixes are different quantities.
Could a very selective gate have a high no-correction rate without resolving the broader commitment problem?

Conceptually, yes. This hypothesis concerns the reliability of prefixes that pass, not how frequently pass decisions occur. A high conditional rate would speak to identifying safe commitments within that selected group; it would not alone establish that enough target output can be committed when needed.
Does “MuST-C En–De” set the language and material to which the prediction applies?

Yes. The hypothesis is specifically about late-resolution MuST-C En–De—English-to-German material in which negation or semantic roles resolve late. It does not assert that the same percentage would hold for other language directions or other material.
Could we say the hypothesis proves that ASR-lattice posteriors identify safe prefixes?

No. It is a proposed prediction, not proof or an observed finding. If the stated threshold were met, it would bear on whether the gate identifies prefixes that do not need oracle correction in the specified setting. The hypothesis itself supplies no measurement showing that it does.
Does it require every passing prefix to remain unchanged?

No. Requiring every passing prefix to need no correction would be a 100% claim. This hypothesis sets the threshold at at least 95% of passing prefixes, leaving room for a minority to need oracle correction.
Could I interpret the remaining percentage as a known error rate?

No rate has been observed here. If the hypothesis held, no more than 5% of passing prefixes would need oracle correction under the stated judgment. That is a consequence of the proposed threshold, not a measured error rate or a claim about prefixes that did not pass.
Is this threshold the same as the goal of at least 20% fewer negation and role errors than a matched-latency streaming baseline?

No. The ≥95% hypothesis concerns oracle correction among prefixes passing a 0.9 gate on late-resolution MuST-C En–De. The goal's at-least-20% requirement compares negation and role errors with a matched-latency streaming baseline. Neither threshold, by itself, establishes the other.
And does this hypothesis establish average lagging below two seconds or overall COMET not decreasing?

No. It makes no claim about measured average lagging or overall COMET. Those remain distinct requirements of the simultaneous-translation goal, even though the gate is relevant to deciding which prefixes might be committed irreversibly.
Where does the 1.8-second hold cap fit in this particular claim?

The hold cap belongs to the proposal for deferring risky phrases. This hypothesis is narrower: it predicts a no-oracle-correction rate for prefixes that pass the 0.9 role-negation lattice gate on late-resolution MuST-C En–De. It does not say that the hold cap has been tested or that it produces the predicted rate.
So the hypothesis answers the open question in a conditional, testable form: if the gate is useful here, at least 95% of what it lets through should not need an oracle to fix it?

That is the intended reading, with the scope kept precise: the prediction is that ≥95% of prefixes passing the 0.9 role-negation lattice gate on late-resolution MuST-C En–De need no oracle correction. Whether that prediction holds, how often prefixes pass, and whether the full latency and translation-quality goals are met are not established by stating it.
How would we evaluate the hypothesis about prefixes passing the role-negation lattice gate?

The activity is to replay MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances through streaming ASR, then measure the prefixes that pass the 0.9 gate and need no oracle correction. The measured share of passing prefixes that are oracle-correction-free is compared with 95%. This describes an evaluation to perform, not one that has already produced a result.
Why replay the utterances through streaming ASR rather than look only at completed utterances?

The question concerns commitments made while speech is unfolding. Replay through streaming ASR keeps the evaluation focused on the information available for a streaming commitment, rather than treating the completed utterance as though it had been available from the start. The activity does not specify the mechanics of that replay.
Are these any MuST-C utterances, or a particular subset?

The activity specifies MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances. That restriction matters because the proposed gate is meant to address prefixes whose correctness could be affected when negation or semantic roles become clear late. The node does not give a selection procedure or a count of utterances.
What is the unit we measure: an utterance, a phrase, or a prefix?

A prefix. More specifically, the stated measurement concerns prefixes passing the 0.9 gate. The utterances provide the material replayed through streaming ASR, but the 95% comparison is about passing prefixes, not the percentage of utterances with no errors.
Can you spell out the fraction without assuming we have any results yet?

The denominator is the prefixes that pass the 0.9 role-negation lattice gate during the specified replay. The numerator is those passing prefixes that need no oracle correction. The activity measures that fraction and compares it against the hypothesized threshold of at least 95%; it does not supply the measured fraction.
Would prefixes rejected by the gate count as correction failures?

Not in this particular fraction. They are outside the group described as “prefixes passing the 0.9 gate.” That does not tell us whether rejected prefixes were right or wrong; it only keeps the measurement aligned with the stated hypothesis.
What if the gate passes very few prefixes?

Then the measured share would still describe only those few passing prefixes. It would not tell us that the gate permits frequent commitments. The activity calls for measuring oracle-correction-free passing prefixes against 95%, but does not specify a separate coverage requirement or how to handle a case with no passing prefixes.
Is the 0.9 a threshold we vary during this activity?

No variation is stated. The activity refers to prefixes passing the 0.9 gate, matching the gate in the hypothesis being evaluated. A comparison across other gate settings would be an additional activity, not something specified here.
And the 95% is not a gate setting?

Correct. The 0.9 identifies the role-negation lattice gate applied to prefixes. The 95% is the benchmark for the measured share of passing prefixes needing no oracle correction. They play different roles in the evaluation.
Does “against 95%” mean the measured share must exceed 95% strictly?

The hypothesis being evaluated says ≥95%, so equality would meet its stated threshold. The activity is to measure the share and compare it with that threshold; it does not say what the measurement will be.
What is the purpose of checking for oracle correction after the prefix has passed?

Passing the gate is the proposed signal that a prefix is safe to commit. Checking whether it needs oracle correction asks whether that signal held up when the late-resolving meaning is taken into account. The measurement therefore tests the gate's proposed ability to select prefixes that can remain committed without correction.
Does the node define how the oracle decides a prefix needs correction?

No. It specifies the outcome to measure—whether passing prefixes are oracle-correction-free—but not an oracle procedure or detailed correction criteria. Those details should not be inferred from the activity as stated.
Would it be accurate to say we are measuring how often the gate's passing decisions are vindicated, not how often it rejects risky wording?

Yes. The stated fraction checks passing prefixes for the absence of an oracle correction. It does not directly measure whether rejected prefixes were risky, or whether some rejected prefixes could have been committed safely.
If later speech resolves negation but not a role ambiguity, does the activity say how that case is classified?

It does not provide case-level classification rules. It names late-resolution MuST-C En–De utterances and the role-negation lattice gate, and asks for the oracle-correction-free share among passing prefixes. We should not invent a rule for particular combinations of late-resolving information.
Should we report separate percentages for negation and semantic roles?

Separate percentages are not specified in this activity. Its stated comparison is the share of oracle-correction-free prefixes passing the 0.9 gate against 95%. Negation and roles explain what the gate addresses, but the node does not call for separate breakdowns.
Could I treat every prefix that needs no correction as proof that the gate understood the entire utterance?
No. The judgment concerns that passing prefix. Needing no oracle correction for it does not establish that the rest of the utterance was translated correctly, or that every later commitment was safe.
Suppose the measured share came out below 95%. What would this activity tell us?

That hypothetical outcome would fall below the stated threshold for the passing-prefix measurement. The activity has not produced such an outcome, and the node does not specify a diagnosis or a change to the gate in that event.
And if it reached at least 95%, would that finish the simultaneous-translation goal?

No. It would address this narrower hypothesis about oracle correction among prefixes passing the gate on late-resolution MuST-C En–De. It would not, by itself, establish how often prefixes can be committed, the system's latency, its comparison on negation and role errors, or its overall translation quality.
Is there any comparison to a streaming baseline in this activity?

No baseline comparison is specified here. The comparison in this activity is between the measured oracle-correction-free share of prefixes passing the 0.9 gate and the 95% hypothesis threshold. That is distinct from evaluating a complete translation system against a baseline.
I want to be careful not to describe a planned measurement as an observation. How would you state it plainly?

Replay MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances through streaming ASR; among prefixes passing the 0.9 role-negation lattice gate, measure the share needing no oracle correction and compare that share with 95%. No measured share, pass count, or conclusion is stated yet.
What was observed for prefixes passing the 0.9 gate?

On 1,200 MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances, 96.1% of prefixes passing the 0.9 gate required no oracle correction. The percentage describes the passing prefixes, not all prefixes in those utterances.
Does 1,200 count prefixes or utterances?
Utterances. The evidence gives 1,200 MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances as the material considered. It does not state how many prefixes were considered or how many passed the gate.
Then I should not say that 96.1% of the 1,200 utterances needed no correction?
Correct. That would change the unit of measurement. The observed 96.1% applies to prefixes passing the 0.9 gate; the 1,200 figure counts utterances.
Can we work out the exact number of prefixes that required no oracle correction?

Not from these figures alone. We would need the number of prefixes that passed the gate to calculate a count. The evidence supplies their percentage requiring no oracle correction, but not the size of that group.
What does “passing the gate” qualify in that sentence?

It qualifies the prefixes included in the percentage. Among prefixes that passed the 0.9 gate, 96.1% required no oracle correction. The statement makes no corresponding percentage claim about prefixes that did not pass.
Is the 0.9 itself the observed correction-free percentage?
No. The 0.9 identifies the gate setting. The observed percentage is 96.1% of prefixes passing that gate requiring no oracle correction. They are different quantities.
What can we say about the remaining passing prefixes?

As a complement to the reported percentage, approximately 3.9% of passing prefixes required oracle correction, subject to the rounding implicit in reporting 96.1%. The evidence does not describe what those corrections involved.
Could those corrections all have been about negation?
The evidence does not say. It gives no breakdown of corrections by negation, semantic roles, or any other category. We cannot assign the remaining share to a particular kind of issue.
Does requiring no oracle correction mean that a complete translation of an utterance was correct?

No. The observation concerns individual prefixes that passed the gate. A prefix requiring no oracle correction does not, by itself, establish the correctness of the complete translation of its utterance.
Does it tell us that every prefix the gate rejected would have required correction?
No. Nothing in the reported 96.1% characterizes rejected prefixes. Some might or might not have required correction; this evidence does not give a rate for them.
How should I phrase the significance for irreversible output without overstating it?

You can say that, in this set of late-resolution utterances, most prefixes passing the 0.9 gate did not require an oracle to correct them. That is relevant to deciding what wording could be committed irreversibly. It does not mean every passing prefix was safe, since some did require correction.
Do we know whether the gate passed prefixes frequently enough to keep output moving?
Not from this observation. The percentage is conditional on a prefix passing. Without a pass count or pass rate, it does not tell us how often the gate allowed a commitment.
And it does not give a latency measurement?
Right. The evidence reports an oracle-correction outcome for passing prefixes, not how long output was delayed or any measured latency.
Could I generalize the 96.1% to other language directions?

That would go beyond the stated evidence. The observation is specifically on 1,200 MuST-C En–De late-resolution utterances. It does not report the corresponding percentage for another language direction or another set of material.
Is this an estimate about all late-resolution MuST-C En–De utterances, or just the reported set?

The stated observation is on the 1,200 utterances. It does not provide sampling details or an uncertainty interval, so the safest wording keeps the 96.1% tied to that reported set rather than asserting a rate for every such utterance.
Could one utterance contribute more than one passing prefix?

The evidence does not give a per-utterance breakdown.
